mutations of the K-RAS and P53 genes can be detected not just in malignant but also non-malignant biopsies of patients with non-small-cell lung cancer.
K-ras and/or p53 mutations were detected in 14 (35 %) of 40 bronchial biopies taken during routine bronchofiberoscopic examination of non-small cell lung carcinoma patients.
mutations of the K- and p53 genes are present in bronchial tissue of patients with non-small lung cancer.

the detection of mutations of the p16, p53, K-ras, and c-erb B-2 genes in bronchial epithelial biopsies taken from patients with lung cancer and non-malignancy.
the detection and analysis of mutations of the p16 gene in non-small cell carcinoma of the lung.
the development of new molecular markers for early detection and therapy of non-small cell lung cancers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the detection of K-ras mutations in bronchial mucosa is not a useful tool in the early detection of bronchial carcinoma.
K-ras and especially p53 gene mutations can be detected in normal appearing lung tissue of patients with NSCLCs.

molecular screening of non-malignant lung tissue for the presence of gene defects in lung cancer patients may be useful in identifying early stages of malignant disease, but the clinical significance and the cost effectiveness of these methods remain to be established.

mutations in non-molecular biopsies are not rare.

molecular screening may increase the probability to detect early malignant lesions in NSCLC patients.
